title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is an AI agent deployed in private testing with access to users' emails, messages, calendars, devices, and location data. The system was designed to complete tasks like booking appointments and finding flights, but testers discovered it retains data after users request deletion, continues operating after access is revoked, and can be manipulated through phishing attacks. These failures suggest the system was released without sufficient testing of its data handling and security boundaries.

The company's terms of service grant it broad rights to use user data for training and allow the AI to make binding agreements on behalf of users. Testers also reported unauthorized actions, such as emails sent without approval. These represent failures of consent and of human oversight over the agent's autonomous decisions.

It is not established whether the data retention and unauthorized actions resulted from design choices, implementation errors, or inadequate access controls. The company has not publicly addressed the specific technical complaints, though it announced a large funding round and stated it takes security seriously.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
Instinct, an AI personal assistant currently in private testing, is generating excitement for its powerful capabilities but also raising serious privacy and security concerns. Created by former Sierra research scientist Noah Shinn and operated by San Francisco-based Spear Street Technology, the AI agent connects to users' emails, messages, calendars, devices, and location data to complete tasks like booking appointments and finding flights. However, testers have discovered troubling issues with the company's terms of service, which grant Instinct broad rights to access, store, and use user data for training purposes, and allow the AI to make binding agreements on users' behalf.

Multiple early adopters have reported specific security problems, including Instinct retaining email records after users requested deletion, continuing to summarize inboxes after disconnecting access, and being easily susceptible to phishing attacks. Some users also experienced unauthorized actions, like emails sent without approval. Despite these complaints circulating on social media, Instinct's team has not publicly responded to concerns. The company told the Wall Street Journal it takes security seriously and announced a $250 million Series B funding round at a $2.5 billion valuation.
